stories.headline: Warsh’s first Jackson Hole speech: inflation still too high, Fed ‘has work to do’
stories.dek: He kept the 2% target ‘firm and fixed,’ skipped forward guidance, and lifted September hike bets from about one-third to a coin flip or better.
stories.caveman: The mountain speech happened. New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh spoke Friday in Wyoming. He said summer inflation numbers looked a bit better but did not prove the trend is really cooling. His line: the Fed must see prices heading to 2 percent clearly and fast. If not, ‘we have work to do.’ He called the 2 percent goal firm and fixed. He would not map the next rate move in advance. He said short-term rates are still the main tool. After the talk, traders raised the chance of a September hike to the mid-to-high 50s, up from about 35 percent Thursday. The 2-year Treasury yield jumped. No vote happens at the lodge. The next real meeting is Sept. 15–16. Jobs and inflation data still land first.
stories.why_it_matters: A new chair’s first Jackson Hole talk sets the mood for mortgages, the dollar, and Asian tech. A hike scare can knock growth stocks before Taipei’s Monday open.
stories.camps: Hawks hear a man willing to raise rates even if the president who picked him wants cuts. Doves say he still left himself room to wait for data. Renters and small borrowers feel the yield jump, not the Wyoming scenery.

terms.explain: The Fed’s yearly mountain meeting. Chairs often sketch how they will fight inflation.
When the Fed tells markets what it will likely do next. Warsh says he does not want to feed that trade.
The inflation number the Fed says it wants. PCE is the price gauge it uses.
Making borrowing cost more so spending slows and prices cool.

stories.image_alt: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaking at the Jackson Hole symposium on CNBC

stories.headline: Wall Street fades Friday after Warsh: S&P 7,712, Nasdaq off 0.5%, Nvidia drops 4.6%
stories.dek: Indexes still finished the week up. Chip stocks gave back Thursday’s Nvidia bounce. Marvell sank 10%.
stories.caveman: Friday was a hangover, not a crash. The S&P 500 fell 0.25 percent to 7,711.76. The Nasdaq lost 0.52 percent to 26,402.42. The Dow barely moved, off 0.02 percent at 53,559.99. For the whole week all three still rose. Nvidia, which had jumped after Wednesday’s giant print, slipped 4.6 percent. Marvell tumbled 10.3 percent even after a record quarter, because investors doubted when Google-related AI chip sales will show up. Apple and Alphabet still rose. PayPal dropped almost 13 percent after a buyout chase was said to be dead. Markets heard Warsh, marked hike odds up, and went home for the weekend.
stories.why_it_matters: Asia inherits a hawkish Fed plus a sold-the-news chip tape. A Friday fade can become Monday’s open in Taipei and Seoul.
stories.camps: Bulls say the week is still green and AI demand is intact. Bears say Warsh just made money more expensive. Factory and warehouse workers do not get the after-hours bounce.

terms.explain: A stock falls after good headlines because the good news was already priced in.
The index still finished higher than last Friday even if the last day slipped.
The handful of huge companies that can lift or sink the whole S&P.

stories.image_alt: Pedestrians outside the New York Stock Exchange

stories.headline: Oil jumps more than 2% Monday; Brent back above $90 after US hits Larak Island
stories.dek: WTI $85.41. Brent $90.32. First known American strikes on Iran since late July, aimed at launchers US officials said were prepping sea mines.
stories.caveman: Crude woke up angry. By Monday morning in Asia, Brent futures were up 2.52 percent at $90.32 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate rose 2.41 percent to $85.41. The spark: US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday. Washington said Revolutionary Guard crews were getting ready to fire rockets with sea mines into the waterway. It is the first known US strike on Iran since late July. Friday’s close had been sleepy — WTI $83.40, Brent $89.31, the first weekly drop in three weeks. That cushion is gone. Pump prices will lag the screen. They always do.
stories.why_it_matters: A Hormuz scare hits inflation math the same week Warsh said prices are still too high. Dearer barrels make a September hike easier to argue.
stories.camps: The US calls it mine prevention. Iran calls it an attack on its territory and vowed a reply. Drivers and food importers pay the risk premium either way.

terms.explain: The global oil sticker price, set in London.
The US oil sticker price.
A narrow water gate for a huge share of seaborne oil. Trouble there moves every barrel.
An explosive left in the water to damage ships. Even the threat raises insurance.

stories.image_alt: An oil tanker on open water

stories.headline: Bessent tells G20 to raise walls against China’s $1.2 trillion surplus as the dollar jumps
stories.dek: Asheville meeting opens Monday. After Warsh, the yen slipped back through 160 per dollar. Bessent called that move ‘pretty contained.’
stories.caveman: The money men meet in North Carolina. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Reuters on Sunday he will push G20 finance chiefs to look again at their trade terms with China. He said the world cannot live with a $1.2 trillion Chinese surplus. Beijing, he said, is trying to export its way out of a weak home economy. The US has already slammed tariffs and banned some Chinese goods, so those goods now flood Europe and Latin America. After Warsh’s hawkish talk, the dollar posted its biggest daily climb in about two and a half months. The yen broke 160 per dollar again, the first time since a late-July intervention. The Philippine peso tagged a record weak 62. Bessent said yen moves still look orderly. Importers may disagree.
stories.why_it_matters: A strong dollar plus talk of more China barriers hits emerging-market currencies, chip demand, and the cost of imported food and fuel.
stories.camps: Washington wants others to share the China squeeze. Beijing says cooperation is legal and talks are the way out. Shoppers in Manila and Tokyo feel the currency first.

terms.explain: A club of big economies. This week they meet in Asheville, North Carolina.
When a country sells a lot more than it buys. China’s number is huge.
A score for how strong the US dollar is against a basket of other currencies.
How many yen one dollar buys. A higher number means a weaker yen.

stories.image_alt: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent arrives in Asheville for the G20 finance meeting

stories.headline: OpenAI will cut off models for SpaceX-owned Cursor, escalating the Altman–Musk feud
stories.dek: Proposed shutoff Nov. 12. Cursor says OpenAI is about 5% of traffic. Anthropic says it will send more Claude compute the other way.
stories.caveman: OpenAI is unplugging a customer. On Friday it said it will stop giving its models to Cursor, the coding tool SpaceX bought this month for about $60 billion. Reason given: it does not trust SpaceX to obey the rules, based on how Elon Musk’s other firms treated contracts. OpenAI also said X broke terms after Musk bought it. The cutoff date on the table is Nov. 12. Cursor co-founder Michael Truell said they are talking and that OpenAI models are only about 5 percent of user traffic. Musk posted that he ‘couldn’t care less.’ Hours later Anthropic said it would add compute so Claude can pick up more of Cursor’s load. Two labs, one coding app, a very public divorce.
stories.why_it_matters: If a model vendor can yank the plug after a change of control, every AI startup just learned its supplier is also a rival with a kill switch.
stories.camps: OpenAI frames safety and contracts. Musk frames a stolen nonprofit and shrugs. Coders just want the autocomplete to keep working.

terms.explain: A popular AI coding app. SpaceX closed a giant stock deal for it this month.
When a company is bought. Contracts often let a vendor walk away after that.
The fine print on how a model may be used. Break them and the vendor can cut the pipe.

stories.image_alt: Sam Altman and Elon Musk in a composite photo from the OpenAI trial

stories.headline: Judge rules Pentagon’s ‘supply-chain risk’ label on Anthropic was illegal retaliation
stories.dek: Rita Lin in California: First Amendment, due process, arbitrary and capricious. The Washington case is still alive.
stories.caveman: Anthropic won a round. A federal judge in California said Thursday night that the Trump administration broke the law when it branded the Claude maker a supply-chain risk and told even non-defense agencies to stop using it. Judge Rita Lin called the move unlawful retaliation for speech, and arbitrary. She said Anthropic got no fair process. The fight started when Anthropic drew hard lines against using its models for fully autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans. The Pentagon said it only wanted lawful use. Lin noted the government still chased a contract and even tried Anthropic’s new Mythos model for cybersecurity — odd behavior toward a supposed threat. A DC lawsuit continues. The Department of War can still pick its vendor. It cannot, she wrote, use ‘national security’ as a blank check to punish critics.
stories.why_it_matters: If a lab can be blacklisted for refusing certain military uses, every safety promise is a business risk. The ruling tests how far a White House can go.
stories.camps: Anthropic calls it a win for lawful process. Hawks say a contractor should not dictate war rules. Civil-liberties groups wanted the surveillance red line kept.

terms.explain: A government stamp that says a vendor is too dangerous to buy from.
Legal talk for a decision that does not match the facts or the rules.
Weapons that pick and hit targets with little human control. Anthropic refused that use.

stories.image_alt: Anthropic logo on a smartphone

stories.headline: Apple rushed new Mac mini and Mac Studio after AI shops emptied the shelves
stories.dek: The Information: enterprise demand surprised Cupertino. Memory shortages leave high-end boxes out of stock. Some buyers walk to Nvidia’s DGX Spark.
stories.caveman: Apple dropped new Mac mini and Mac Studio boxes earlier than usual. Not for the September iPhone show. For AI. The Information says companies want desk-side Macs to run big models, and Apple did not see the rush coming. It even showed how several Mac Studios can be chained together. It still lacks a real enterprise AI team. Firms that asked to buy into Apple’s Private Cloud Compute were turned down. Partners such as WebAI and Mount Thor fill the gap. A global memory shortage means many configs are sold out for months. Some customers are switching to Nvidia’s small DGX Spark instead. Tim Cook hands the CEO chair to John Ternus on Sept. 1. The first hardware surprise of the new era is a computer, not a phone.
stories.why_it_matters: If Apple cannot ship Macs, Nvidia wins another desktop. Memory shortages also tie the same supply chain that feeds Taiwan’s fabs.
stories.camps: Apple calls it a feature for developers. Critics say the company still treats business as an afterthought. IT buyers just want a box that is in stock.

terms.explain: Apple’s small, powerful desktop. Companies now chain several to run large AI models.
Apple’s locked-down cloud for AI. The report says it would not sell access to outside firms.
Not enough chips that store working data. High-end Macs and AI servers fight for the same parts.

stories.image_alt: Two Apple Mac Studio computers

stories.headline: Marvell posts a record $2.74 billion quarter, then falls 10% on Google AI timing doubts
stories.dek: Data-center sales up 46%. Outlook raised. Friday still punished the stock after Nvidia’s glow faded.
stories.caveman: Marvell did the homework and still got sent to the hallway. The chip firm reported record fiscal-second-quarter sales of $2.739 billion, up 37 percent from a year ago. Data center grew 46 percent. The boss said AI bookings are strong and raised the sales map for this year and next. Custom chips for big customers, including work tied to Google, are supposed to accelerate in the second half. Investors wanted the money sooner. On Friday Marvell dropped 10.3 percent. Nvidia, the week’s star, slipped 4.6 percent the same day. Record sales are not enough when the tape is already tired.
stories.why_it_matters: Marvell is a tell for AI networking and custom silicon, not just Nvidia’s GPU story. A 10 percent drop after a beat is a warning about how picky this rally has become.
stories.camps: Management says demand is broad. Bears say Google revenue is late and the stock had already doubled. Engineers shipping the chips still work the same hours.

terms.explain: Chips built for one giant customer, not sold off the shelf. Google is in this story.
Sales into the warehouses that train and run AI. This is Marvell’s growth engine.
What the company says future sales might be. Markets trade the guide as hard as the past quarter.

stories.image_alt: Marvell Technology logo over a circuit-board graphic

stories.headline: US strikes Iranian launchers on Larak Island; Tehran says it fired on two US bases in Jordan
stories.dek: First known American hits on Iran since late July. Washington says the launchers were being readied with sea mines for Hormuz.
stories.caveman: The pause broke. A US official said American forces hit two Iranian launchers on Larak Island on Sunday. The island sits in the Strait of Hormuz. The official said Revolutionary Guard teams were preparing rockets with sea mines. Iranian media called it a drone strike. On Monday Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they launched ballistic missiles at the King Hussein and Al Azraq US bases in Jordan in reply. Trump had paused a two-week campaign in late July. This is the first known US strike on Iran since then. The wider war is six months old. Diplomacy over who ‘opens’ Hormuz is still stuck.
stories.why_it_matters: A new strike-and-reply loop can close shipping, lift oil, and pull US bases in Jordan back onto the map. It also lands on the same Monday as Warsh’s hike scare.
stories.camps: Washington says it stopped a mining attempt. Tehran says the strait is still under its rules and vows revenge. Jordan hosts the bases and did not ask for the crossfire. Tanker crews want a lane, not a press release.

terms.explain: Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz. A military perch over the oil lane.
Iran’s powerful military-political force. Its navy has been the face of Hormuz policy.
A rocket that flies a high arc and comes down hard. Used here against bases in Jordan.

stories.image_alt: Two fighter jets over desert terrain

stories.headline: CIA chief Ratcliffe proposed a Trump–Putin–Zelensky summit during a covert Moscow trip
stories.dek: He met Russia’s spy bosses. Zelensky was briefed Friday. Putin has rejected a three-way meeting before.
stories.caveman: The spy chief went to Moscow. CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a quiet trip this week and, Axios reports, floated a three-president meeting: Trump, Putin, Zelensky. He sat with Sergey Naryshkin of foreign intelligence and Alexander Bortnikov of the FSB. Sources said he wanted to know if those men could nudge Putin back to US-mediated talks. US officials briefed Zelensky on Friday. Zelensky has liked the summit idea before. Putin has said no. Trump called the visit standard or ‘semi-routine’ and denied it was mainly a NATO warning. The New York Times said Ratcliffe gave Bortnikov a bleak picture of the war and urged a deal before Russia’s position gets worse. Ukraine’s chief of staff has talked about talks in September. Nothing is booked.
stories.why_it_matters: A CIA director doing diplomacy means White House envoys have not closed a path. Civilians still live under the drones while the seating chart is argued.
stories.camps: Kyiv wants a table that does not trade away land in the dark. The Kremlin wants terms it has already refused. People in the blast radius are not in the room.

terms.explain: A sit-down with three leaders at once. Here: US, Russia, Ukraine.
Russia’s main domestic security agency. Ratcliffe treated its boss as a possible channel.
Negotiations where Washington tries to carry messages both ways.

stories.image_alt: Russian President Vladimir Putin in a formal setting

stories.headline: Zelensky says Ukraine is lining up fresh talks with Trump envoys
stories.dek: ‘War must not remain the only option.’ He said America shares many of Kyiv’s views on the front and on strikes. Details due Monday.
stories.caveman: Kyiv is putting names on a calendar. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday his team is preparing new talks with people from Donald Trump’s office. More detail, he said, would come Monday. His line: do everything so war is not the only next chapter. He added that the United States shares many Ukrainian views on the front and on strikes. The comment lands after the CIA director’s Moscow visit and after US officials briefed him on a possible three-way summit. Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have already shuttled for months with little to show. Zelensky is signaling he will stay at the table even while drones keep coming.
stories.why_it_matters: If talks restart in September, the terms will be written while cities are still being hit. A pause in talking is also a political choice.
stories.camps: Zelensky wants US leverage without a dictated peace. Trump wants a deal he can claim. Russians living under Ukrainian strikes, and Ukrainians under Russian ones, do not pick the agenda.

terms.explain: People sent by a president to talk when the presidents are not in the same room.
Where the armies actually meet. Sharing ‘views on the front’ means agreeing, or not, on who is winning.
Missiles and drones aimed deep behind the line. Both sides do this. Civilians die in both.

stories.image_alt: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky speaking at a podium

stories.headline: Iran’s president says war and US ‘economic D-Day’ have cut trade by a third
stories.dek: Inflation 66%. Supreme Leader tells the government to fix prices and jobs. Washington adds weekly secondary sanctions; China is so far spared the bank hammer.
stories.caveman: Tehran is saying the quiet part. President Masoud Pezeshkian told state media that exports and imports are down about 35 percent because of US sanctions and a naval blockade. Annual inflation hit 66 percent last month. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since he was hurt in the February opening attack that killed his father, issued a written call to tackle prices, jobs, and markets. He is not offering a retreat on Hormuz. The US is branding the squeeze ‘economic D-Day’ and warning other countries to drop Iran business. Treasury hit Egypt’s Banque Misr over its UAE unit’s dollar trades. China and India have not faced the full bank ban — yet. Trump has hinted they could. Qatar’s prime minister was in Tehran last week pushing to reopen the strait. Pezeshkian wants the short June memorandum revived. It fell apart over who controls Hormuz.
stories.why_it_matters: Sanctions are now the main US lever while the strait stays contested. Ordinary Iranians pay 66 percent inflation. Global food and fuel still ride the same water.
stories.camps: Washington says pain will force a deal. Tehran says diplomacy and defense are two wings of the same bird. Shoppers in Iran and shippers outside it are not at the table.

terms.explain: US plan to punish not only Iran but firms in other countries that still trade with it.
Penalties on a bank or ship in, say, Egypt or Hong Kong, for dealing with Iran.
A short June paper that paused fighting and promised some oil sales. It collapsed over Hormuz control.

stories.image_alt: An oil tanker at sea

stories.headline: Romantasy’s Poison Daughter debuts at No. 1 on Publishers Weekly’s hardcover fiction list
stories.dek: Sheila Masterson’s Slowburn edition lands the week Hulu is developing a series. She started by self-publishing.
stories.caveman: A poison kiss just took the top shelf. Publishers Weekly’s Aug. 31 chart puts The Poison Daughter by Sheila Masterson at No. 1 hardcover fiction. It is the Slowburn edition of a 2025 book that first exploded on social media. Masterson self-published a romantasy called The Lost God in 2023. Slowburn bought this one in April. Hulu said earlier this month it is developing a series. The plot: a woman’s lips are deadly until she meets the man who can survive the kiss. Enemies, then lovers, then a streaming pitch. Independent bookstores already logged it as a new IndieBound entry. TikTok did the marketing. The publisher cashed the check.
stories.why_it_matters: When a self-pub romantasy leapfrogs prestige names, it shows who actually moves hardcover copies in 2026: fandom, not only reviews.
stories.camps: Fans wanted the special edition and the show. Some literary desks still roll their eyes at ‘romantasy.’ Bookstore staff order what walks out the door.

terms.explain: Love story plus magic. Huge on social media. Often first sold by the author, then picked up.
A weekly ranking of new clothbound novels by print sales, not vibes.
The publisher that bought Masterson’s hit and put it in stores this week.

stories.image_alt: Book cover of The Poison Daughter by Sheila Masterson

stories.headline: Quiet sleeper Theo of Golden tops the new NYT combined fiction list; Yesteryear slips to No. 4
stories.dek: Allen Levi’s late-life debut — a man who buys coffee-shop portraits and gives them back — is still the book America is buying.
stories.caveman: Kindness is still outselling the tradwife nightmare. The New York Times combined print-and-ebook fiction list dated Aug. 28 puts Theo of Golden by Allen Levi at No. 1. Kathryn Stockett’s The Calamity Club is No. 2. Caro Claire Burke’s Yesteryear, last issue’s IndieBound king, sits at No. 4. Levi was nearly 70, an ex-lawyer and musician in Georgia, when friends pushed him to self-publish in 2023. Simon & Schuster’s Atria later took it. The story: a mysterious older man walks into a town like Columbus, buys portraits off a coffeehouse wall, and returns each one to the person in the picture. No spies. No poison kiss. Reports this month put US sales in the millions and movie talks around Tom Hanks. On this chart, the quiet book is still first.
stories.why_it_matters: Lists are a fight between comfort, satire, and romantasy. When a gentle debut holds No. 1, it tells shops what readers reach for when the news is loud.
stories.camps: Readers call it an antidote. Skeptics call it syrup. Levi did not write it as a culture-war object. Booksellers just restock it.

terms.explain: One ranking that adds paper books and digital copies. A paperback and a Kindle sale both count.
A book that grows by word of mouth, not a giant ad blast on week one.
The tradwife-in-1855 satire that led last week’s indie list. It did not lead this NYT combined list.

stories.image_alt: Book cover of Theo of Golden by Allen Levi

stories.headline: Pardon My Book, a Barstool sports-podcast dump, opens at No. 1 nonfiction
stories.dek: Dan ‘Big Cat’ Katz and Eric ‘PFT Commenter’ Sollenberger outsold Dave Portnoy’s own recent hit. They brag about the spelling.
stories.caveman: The other chart is not shy. Publishers Weekly’s hardcover nonfiction No. 1 this week is Pardon My Book, from the duo behind Barstool Sports’ Pardon My Take podcast. They are marking 10 years of the show. PW says it sold about 14,000 more print copies than Dave Portnoy’s Cancel Me If You Can did on its own debut. Katz admitted to ‘some god-awful writing.’ Sollenberger said they care more about telling than spelling. That is the product. It is a reminder that US nonfiction lists still have a loud, male, sports-comedy lane next to the serious books.
stories.why_it_matters: Charts are not a library. They are a register of what people pay for. A podcast script at No. 1 shows the power of an existing audience.
stories.camps: Fans wanted a souvenir of the show. Critics see the death of copyediting. Bookstore workers still have to shelve it next to the reported books.

terms.explain: Weekly ranking of fact-shaped books in cloth covers, including memoirs, politics, and joke books.
A loud US sports-and-comedy company. Portnoy founded it. This podcast is its biggest.
When a hit audio show becomes a physical book aimed at the same fans.

stories.image_alt: Book cover of Pardon My Book by Big Cat and PFT Commenter

stories.headline: The Nerd Reich, a takedown of Trump-aligned tech billionaires, hits No. 6 nonfiction
stories.dek: Gil Durán’s starred debut asks: billionaires or democracy? It is climbing the same PW list as the Barstool joke book.
stories.caveman: A harsher book is also moving. Gil Durán’s The Nerd Reich is No. 6 on this week’s PW hardcover nonfiction list. Publishers Weekly gave it a starred review: a ‘transfixing debut’ on the antidemocratic ideas of tech billionaires tied to the second Trump administration. Durán told PW people have been slow to see how radical those men became and how much power they are taking. His sound bite: the world has billions of people and a few thousand billionaires, and it will not get both billionaire rule and democracy. On the same chart, a sports podcast is No. 1 and this investigation is No. 6. That is the US nonfiction split in one photo.
stories.why_it_matters: Who is hot is not only romantasy. Political nonfiction about tech power is selling in the same week the White House fights AI labs in court.
stories.camps: Durán wants a public that picks democracy. The billionaire class calls this moral panic. Readers who live under both the apps and the administration are the market.

terms.explain: A trade-magazine extra-strong recommend. It does not guarantee sales. This time sales followed.
A small set of very rich men from Silicon Valley with political projects, not just products.
A first book of reported argument, not a novel. Durán is a journalist.

stories.image_alt: Book cover of The Nerd Reich by Gil Durán

stories.headline: UN: four children killed in Gaza this week; a strike wrecked $770,000 in nutrition stocks
stories.dek: UNICEF says the food was meant for more than 45,000 children and mothers. A well serving 4,000 people in Deir al-Balah was also hit.
stories.caveman: The ceasefire on paper is not a ceasefire in kitchens. OCHA said Friday Israeli attacks killed four children, ages 2 to 16, in separate strikes. One child died of wounds from last week. UNICEF said a nearby strike heavily damaged a UN partner warehouse and destroyed more than $770,000 of nutrition supplies meant for over 45,000 children, pregnant women, and breastfeeding mothers. A UNICEF-supported well and desalination plant in Deir al-Balah, serving more than 4,000 people, was badly damaged Monday. Water is now trucked. A munition exploded about 30 meters from a UN fuel convoy at the Yellow Line in Rafah on Thursday. No one in the convoy died. WHO got 106 patients out last week. Thousands still wait. The UN still has no green light to bring in gear to clear unexploded bombs.
stories.why_it_matters: Killing children and burning therapeutic food is not a side effect. It is how a hungry place gets hungrier, even after a deal that was supposed to stop the two-year war.
stories.camps: Israel says it is hitting militants and keeping a right to self-defense. The UN says civilians and aid sites must be protected. Parents in Gaza need formula, water, and a night without drones.

terms.explain: Special food and supplements for hungry children and new mothers. Not the same as a regular grocery sack.
A military dividing line in Gaza. Crossing it with aid still takes permission and luck.
Moving a wounded or sick person out of Gaza for treatment. The queue is still thousands long.

stories.image_alt: A child holds a homemade kite on a damaged street in Gaza

stories.headline: WHO counts 3,205 attacks on Ukraine’s health system; six aid warehouses hit this month
stories.dek: Overnight strikes killed at least 12 civilians. UNICEF lost a Kyiv-region warehouse of winter-bound supplies.
stories.caveman: Hospitals are a target set. WHO’s man in Ukraine said Friday there have been 3,205 attacks on health care since Russia’s full-scale invasion. In 2026 alone, 20 attacks hit humanitarian warehouses, 13 of them storing medicine. WHO already lost stocks in Kyiv in July and Dnipro in August meant to help 225,000 people. Overnight strikes into Friday killed at least 12 civilians and hurt more than 65. UNICEF said a warehouse in the Kyiv region was hit, wrecking aid needed before winter. The UN spokesman said at least six humanitarian warehouses were hit this month. WHO is still running convoys into hard-to-reach towns and installing heaters in clinics. A quarter of doctors and nurses show depression symptoms. Winter is the next deadline.
stories.why_it_matters: When warehouses burn, the harm lands in January: no medicine, no heat, no kits. Counting 3,205 health attacks is how you prove a pattern, not a one-off.
stories.camps: Kyiv and the UN call it a campaign against civilians. Moscow denies or blames Ukrainian storage. Patients in the dark clinics do not care who won the briefing.

terms.explain: Hits on clinics, ambulances, or medical stores. International law says these are protected.
A shed or hall full of medicine, food, or winter kits. Six of them were hit in Ukraine this month.
Trucks carrying medical goods with UN markings. They still need permission and intact roads.

stories.image_alt: A building on fire at night after a strike in Ukraine

stories.headline: Armed raid on a South Sudan cattle camp kills at least 49, wounds 33
stories.dek: Warrap State, Thursday. Local officials blame a cross-border armed network. A raid three weeks ago in the same area killed 60.
stories.caveman: Another dawn, another cattle camp. Officials in Warrap State, South Sudan, said gunmen attacked the Machar-Pakuek cattle camp and the village of Mading Juer Boma early Thursday. At least 49 people were killed and 33 wounded. The state spokesman called it a cross-border criminal network and asked aid groups to help people forced to run. Herders fight over grass and water. This is the second mass killing in the same area in three weeks — the earlier raid left 60 dead. President Salva Kiir declared a six-month state of emergency last year over these cycles. The UN mission’s chief already flagged Warrap this month. Restraint is the official word. The graves are the fact.
stories.why_it_matters: South Sudan’s civilian deaths rarely lead global newscasts. A 49-person raid, on top of 60, is a humanitarian emergency even without a front-page war logo.
stories.camps: Local government blames outside gunmen and asks for aid. Communities want grazing land and safety, not another emergency declaration. Women and children in the camp did not pick the feud.

terms.explain: A temporary herding site. Families sleep next to the animals. That makes raids deadly.
A region in northwest South Sudan hit by repeated communal raids.
A government order that expands police and army power. Kiir used one last year. The raids did not stop.

stories.headline: UN: 58% of Gazans face severe shelter gaps as winter rain nears and aid stocks run dry
stories.dek: Two-thirds of the Strip is still hard to reach. The 2026 flash appeal is only 40% funded. Coordinators say rainy-season kits are planned but not in the warehouses.
stories.caveman: Winter is coming to tents. In a Friday situation report, the UN humanitarian office said 58 percent of people in Gaza face severe or catastrophic shelter gaps — not enough walls, roofs, or household goods to stay safe. About two-thirds of the Strip is still off-limits or tightly restricted, so families stay packed in insecure spots. The humanitarian coordinator told the Security Council that rainy-season plans exist, but shelter stocks are depleted, Israel still limits what can enter, and the 2026 flash appeal is only 40 percent funded. He said soon winter will descend. Airstrikes this period also hit civilian areas and aid sites. In the West Bank, the same report counted more settler attacks and the seizure of UNRWA’s Kalandia training centre in East Jerusalem, putting 340 refugee students at risk. The people in the tents cannot vote on any of this.
stories.why_it_matters: Killing makes the day’s headline. A missing tarp before the rains is how children get sick next month. Funding at 40 percent means the plan on paper is not a roof.
stories.camps: The UN wants crossings, kits, and money now. Israel says it still runs security and access. Families in damaged homes need plastic sheeting, not another conference quote.

terms.explain: An emergency fundraising ask. 40 percent funded means most of the requested money has not arrived.
People without a safe roof, walls, or basic household goods. Tents and wrecked rooms count.
Military limits on where civilians and aid can go. Two-thirds of Gaza is still in this bind.
